one_line_reason: Multiple meta-analyses of RCTs show oral fennel (Foeniculum vulgare) affecting primary dysmenorrhea pain and menopausal symptoms, the exact women's-health outcomes fennel supplements are marketed for.

selected.population: women with primary dysmenorrhea (12 studies pooled)
selected.intervention: Foeniculum vulgare (fennel) oral, vs placebo and vs mefenamic acid (NSAID)
selected.dose_as_stated: not stated (meta-analysis pools multiple RCT doses)
selected.why_selected: Meta-analysis (7 articles for the placebo comparison) showing fennel significantly reduced pain intensity vs placebo, with no significant difference from mefenamic acid

selected.population: women with primary dysmenorrhea (12 studies pooled, 468-502 participants depending on comparison)
selected.intervention: Foeniculum vulgare (fennel) oral, vs placebo and vs conventional drug therapy
selected.why_selected: Independent meta-analysis corroborating a favorable effect of fennel vs placebo (similar to conventional drug therapy), though with very high heterogeneity (I2=98%) that the authors themselves flag

selected.population: menopausal women (7 RCTs pooled, n=145 for the placebo comparison)
selected.intervention: fennel (Foeniculum vulgare Miller) oral, various treatment forms, vs placebo
selected.primary_outcome: menopausal symptom severity; secondary outcomes sexual function, quality of life, psychological health
selected.why_selected: Meta-analysis found fennel significantly improved overall menopausal symptoms vs placebo, but other included studies failed to show benefit for sexual function, quality of life, or psychological health

blockers: None of the three selected meta-analyses states a single consistent oral dose or preparation form in the abstract, which will need resolution against the underlying primary RCTs before mapping to a catalog label amount
33182553's headline placebo-comparison result carries very high statistical heterogeneity (I2=98%), which the review authors flag themselves

excluded_pmids.reason: Pools 5 different Apiaceae-family herbs (anise, dill, cumin, fennel, etc.) for dysmenorrhea; abstract as retrieved does not separate fennel-specific effect estimates from the other 4 herbs
In vitro/in silico screen of plant-based HSP90 inhibitors in breast cancer cell models; not a human trial

General review of herbal remedies for PCOS covering many plants (aloe, chamomile, Vitex, licorice, ginseng, cinnamon, Stachys, fennel); fennel's specific effect is not isolated in the retrieved abstract text
Sustainability/land-footprint meta-analysis of essential oil biopesticide production; agricultural/environmental study, not a human health outcome
Reviews many phytoestrogens (Pueraria mirifica, fennel, hops, soy, red clover, black cohosh, etc.) pooled together for urogenital menopause symptoms; fennel's individual result is not isolated

Western herbal medicines for IBS review dominated by peppermint oil trials; the one relevant trial used aniseed (Pimpinella anisum), a different Apiaceae species from fennel (Foeniculum vulgare), not fennel itself
Cochrane review of oral galactagogues broadly; the retrieved abstract does not state fennel-specific trial results separate from other galactagogues

Pools cinnamon, fennel, and ginger trials together for dysmenorrhea; while a fennel-specific WMD is given, the reported confidence interval (0.119-6.829) appears internally inconsistent/unreliable as retrieved, and the same fennel-dysmenorrhea evidence is better represented by 34187122 and 33182553
